[PAPER_0042, relevance_score=0.301] Regarding the relation between WM capacity and the temporal compression of episodic memories, we formulated two hypotheses.

Hypothesis 1: Our main hypothesis was that a higher WM capacity would enable the recall of more and longer experience units and thus be associated with lower temporal compression rates.

Hypothesis 2: However, people with higher WM capacity could be faster at retrieving experience units, which would reduce the time needed to mentally replay the videos and thus be associated with apparently higher temporal compression rates.

[PAPER_0043, relevance_score=0.295] To disentangle these two hypotheses, we examined estimates of the time needed to remember an experience unit (i.e., the total duration of memory replay divided by the number of recalled experience units). Indeed, according to Hypothesis 1, WM capacity should be positively associated with the duration of remembered experience units, whereas Hypothesis 2 predicted a negative relationship.

We also expected our episodic memory measures to differ according to the segmental structure of events, such that we would observe a higher number of recalled experience units for videos that contained more EBs.

[PAPER_0045, relevance_score=0.341] Thus, we expected to observe an interaction between the density of EBs within videos and WM capacity, such that the magnitude of the difference between high and low EBs videos would be positively associated with WM capacity.

These hypotheses, as well as the methodological design and planned analyses, were preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; https://osf.io/jt9ph).
items.paper_content_summary: Experiment 1 predicted more recalled units and lower compression with higher working-memory capacity, alongside an alternative faster-retrieval hypothesis. It also predicted effects of event-boundary density and its interaction with working memory. The paper additionally predicted a positive working-memory association with unit duration and a working-memory effect on compression controlling for unit count [PAPER_0041] [PAPER_0042] [PAPER_0043] [PAPER_0044] [PAPER_0045] [PAPER_0088].

[PREREG_0017, relevance_score=0.297] Therefore, we hypothesize that WM capacity is positively associated with the number of recalled actions.

Regarding the relation between WM capacity and TCE, we formulate two hypotheses:

(1) our main hypothesis is that a higher WM capacity would enable the remembering of many experience units, leading to longer mental replay durations and thus lower TCE rates.

(2) nevertheless, it is possible that people with better WM abilities are faster at retrieving EUs in episodic memory (which could reduce the time needed to remember videos and thus lead to higher TCE rates).

[PREREG_0018, relevance_score=0.233] To disentangle these two hypotheses, we will not only focus on the relation between WM capacity and TCE (i.e., the ratio between video duration and the duration of its mental replay), but also on estimates of the time needed to remember an action (i.e., the total duration of memory replay divided by the number of recalled actions). If hypothesis 2 is correct, this should be reflected in a negative association between WM capacity and the time needed to remember an action.

We also expect to observe an interaction between the density of EBs and WM capacity.

[PREREG_0064, relevance_score=0.278] Three mixed-effects models will be run, with the following outcome variable: TCE rates, the number of recalled actions, estimation of the time needed to remember an action.

We will also run another mixed-effects model evaluating if the number of recalled actions predict TCE (as shown in previous studies; Folville et al., 2020; Jeunehomme et al., 2020; Jeunehomme & D'Argembeau, 2020) and will further explore whether this interacts with WM capacity.
items.registration_content_summary: The registration predicted more recalled actions and lower compression for videos with more event boundaries, a negative association between action count and compression, and stronger boundary effects with higher working-memory capacity. It predicted more actions and lower compression with higher capacity, with faster retrieval and higher compression as an alternative [PREREG_0016] [PREREG_0017] [PREREG_0018] [PREREG_0019].
items.deviation_information:
The paper adds a directional prediction that working-memory capacity is positively associated with duration per recalled unit under the main hypothesis; the registration specifies a negative association for the alternative but does not predict a positive association for the main hypothesis [PAPER_0043] [PREREG_0017] [PREREG_0018]. The paper also predicts that working memory should remain a significant compression predictor controlling for unit count; this prediction was not found in the provided registration excerpts [PAPER_0088] [PREREG_0064]. The other stated directional predictions are consistent [PAPER_0041] [PAPER_0042] [PAPER_0044] [PAPER_0045] [PREREG_0016] [PREREG_0017] [PREREG_0018] [PREREG_0019].

[PAPER_0071, relevance_score=0.315] Data Cleaning

When using complex span tasks to evaluate WM capacity, it is recommended to exclude participants who show poor performance on the processing part of the tasks (to avoid including participants who neglected the processing part of the tasks; Conway et al., 2005). Following the approach of Gonthier et al. (2016), we excluded participants whose processing accuracy was below the fifth lower percentile of the sample for one of the three tasks (see the online supplemental materials for more detail).

[PAPER_0072, relevance_score=0.284] Regarding the temporal compression task, following our preregistered plan, we excluded from the analyses: (a) all experimental trials for which the difference between the video's duration of presentation and its real duration was greater than 3 s (to remove trials in which the video was not displayed correctly), and (b) trials with a duration of mental replay less than 2 s (i.e., to remove trials during which the participant inadvertently pressed the button twice or did not properly follow the instructions).

[PAPER_0073, relevance_score=0.345] If more than half of trials of one type (high or low density of EBs) had to be excluded for a given participant, the entire participant was excluded and replaced.

[PAPER_0075, relevance_score=0.422] Our main hypotheses were tested using linear mixed-effects models (Brown, 2021). We fitted three models with the following outcome variables: temporal compression rates, the number of recalled experience units, and the duration of recalled experience units. Three predictors were included in all models: (a) participants' WM composite score, which was a continuous predictor varying between subjects, (b) the EB density of videos, which was a dichotomous within-subjects predictor, and (c) their interaction.

[PAPER_0076, relevance_score=0.339] We also ran another mixed-effects model evaluating if the number of recalled experience units predicted temporal compression rates (this model also included EB density, WM score, and their interaction as predictors). In all models, EB density was coded as -0.5 and 0.5, WM score was standardized, and the number of recalled experience units was centered at the participant level (Brauer & Curtin, 2018; Schielzeth, 2010).

As the application conditions of classical linear mixed-effects models were not met, we used a robust alternative.

[PAPER_0077, relevance_score=0.410] We estimated our models with the DAStau procedure implemented in the robustlmm package (Koller, 2016). This method enables to handle both within- and between-participants outliers as well as missing values (Koller, 2013). Equations were estimated with the smoothed Hubber function (Koller, 2013).

When using complex span tasks to evaluate WM capacity, it is recommended to exclude participants who show poor performance on the processing part of the tasks (to avoid including participants who neglected the processing part of the tasks; Conway et al., 2005). [PAPER_0076, relevance_score=0.251] We also ran another mixed-effects model evaluating if the number of recalled experience units predicted temporal compression rates (this model also included EB density, WM score, and their interaction as predictors). As the application conditions of classical linear mixed-effects models were not met, we used a robust alternative.

Participants received a URL (on their prolific account) allowing them to take part in the experiment through Gorilla ((https://gorilla.sc/), a platform providing reliable reaction times measures for online studies (A. Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2021; A. L. Anwyl-Irvine et al., 2020). They were asked to perform the tasks in a quiet and distraction-free environment and were informed that they must complete all tasks (in their entirety) to receive the monetary compensation.

When using complex span tasks to evaluate WM capacity, it is recommended to exclude participants who show poor performance on the processing part of the tasks (to avoid including participants who neglected the processing part of the tasks; Conway et al., 2005). Following the approach of Gonthier et al. (2016), we excluded participants whose processing accuracy was below the fifth lower percentile of the sample for one of the three tasks (see the online supplemental materials for more detail).

[PAPER_0072, relevance_score=0.324] Regarding the temporal compression task, following our preregistered plan, we excluded from the analyses: (a) all experimental trials for which the difference between the video's duration of presentation and its real duration was greater than 3 s (to remove trials in which the video was not displayed correctly), and (b) trials with a duration of mental replay less than 2 s (i.e., to remove trials during which the participant inadvertently pressed the button twice or did not properly follow the instructions).

[PAPER_0073, relevance_score=0.382] If more than half of trials of one type (high or low density of EBs) had to be excluded for a given participant, the entire participant was excluded and replaced.

[PAPER_0077, relevance_score=0.357] We estimated our models with the DAStau procedure implemented in the robustlmm package (Koller, 2016). This method enables to handle both within- and between-participants outliers as well as missing values (Koller, 2013). Equations were estimated with the smoothed Hubber function (Koller, 2013).
